questions.question: How can the database find a variable-length attribute without scanning all the earlier attribute values?
requiredFacts: A fixed-size initial part describes each variable-length attribute using offset and length.
The values themselves follow the initial part; offset locates the value and length bounds it.
reject: Every preceding value must be scanned.

questions.question: Why can storing department and instructor records together speed up their join but slow down a scan of just department?
requiredFacts: Related records share a block or nearby blocks, reducing join reads.
Interleaving leaves fewer department records per block, requiring more reads for department alone.

questions.question: When records move during slotted-page compaction, how do references to those records remain valid?
requiredFacts: References point to stable header or slot entries, not directly to record bytes.
Record locations in those entries are updated as records move, keeping free space contiguous.
reject: All external references must be rewritten.

questions.question: Why is column-oriented storage attractive for analytics but less convenient for updating or reconstructing an entire row?
requiredFacts: Analytics can read only needed columns, with compression as an additional advantage.
A complete row spans separate column structures, adding reconstruction or compressed-update work.
reject: Every analytic query benefits regardless of accessed columns.

questions.question: In a nested-loop join that repeatedly scans an inner relation larger than the buffer, why can LRU perform poorly, and how can the known access pattern help?
requiredFacts: LRU can evict the early inner blocks that will be needed again when the next scan restarts.
Once a block is processed its next use may be far away; MRU can evict that recent block while keeping earlier blocks.
Replacement should use known query access behavior rather than universally assume recency predicts reuse.
reject: MRU is always better for every database workload.

questions.question: If the buffer manager already uses LRU, why must a process still pin a block before reading or modifying it?
requiredFacts: LRU is a victim-selection policy; pinning prevents an in-use frame from being replaced.
Replacement during access could return unrelated data or corrupt the replacement block.
Eviction requires all holders to unpin, commonly tracked by a zero pin count.
reject: Pinning alone prevents concurrent modifications like an exclusive lock.
A recent access guarantees safety until the process finishes.

questions.question: How does a sparse index find a record whose search-key value has no entry in the index, and what ordering does it require?
requiredFacts: Find the greatest indexed search key less than or equal to the desired key, then scan from there.
The data file must be ordered on that search key; fewer index entries save space but add scanning.
reject: A missing sparse index entry proves the record does not exist.

questions.question: Why must a secondary index be dense even though a clustering index can be sparse?
requiredFacts: The file is not ordered on the secondary search key, so scanning from a neighboring indexed key cannot locate omitted keys reliably.
All secondary search-key values need representation, with record pointers or buckets for duplicates.
reject: A dense index necessarily requires one distinct entry per record even with duplicate keys.

questions.question: Why does a B+ tree usually need fewer disk reads than a balanced binary search tree for a million indexed values?
requiredFacts: Disk-block-sized B+ nodes have high fanout, producing a shorter tree.
The example contrasts about four B+ node accesses with about twenty binary-tree node accesses, assuming separate blocks.
A cached root can reduce actual disk reads further.
reject: A balanced binary search tree is unbalanced.
Every B+ lookup is one disk read.

questions.question: For a B+ tree range query, why can finding consecutive leaf entries be cheap while fetching their matching records is still expensive?
requiredFacts: Find the lower bound once, then follow ordered leaf entries and links until the upper bound.
An unclustered secondary index may point to records on different blocks, causing up to one random I/O per match.
Clustering puts matching records together and reduces that record-fetch cost.
reject: Linked index leaves guarantee the actual records are physically contiguous.
